newsitem.title: UK: Sun helps butterflies navigate, study shows.
newsitem.headline: Sun helps butterflies navigate, study shows.

text.p: Scouts and sailors may pride themselves on their abilities to navigate using the sun, but butterflies can do it too, scientists reported on Wednesday.
Tests on Monarch butterflies showed they used the sun as a compass when flying the 4,000 km (2,400 miles) from their autumn breeding grounds in the eastern United States south to Mexico.

Sandra Perez of the department of evolutionary biology at the University of Arizona and colleagues at the University of Kansas threw off the internal body clocks of some butterflies by keeping them in the dark.
In theory, that should throw them off track because the sun would appear to be in the wrong place for the time of day the butterflies thought it was.
This was indeed what happened, the scientists reported in a letter to the science journal Nature.
"We ran behind and beneath butterflies to estimate body orientations (headings) maintained for 15 seconds or more, using hand-held compasses," they wrote.
The mixed-up butterflies were off course to the degree expected, they added.
"The Monarch butterfly thus joins the small group of species for which a sun compass orientation mechanism has been demonstrated experimentally," they wrote.
But the butterflies still managed to navigate correctly on cloudy days, indicating they had a back-up navigational system such as a geomagnetic compass.
